alt: Events reach the reader only through the narrator. If the narrator is trustworthy we accept the picture; if not, we read between and against its words. Reliability shapes what we believe happened and how we judge the people involved.
caption: Everything the reader learns passes through the narrator, so reliability changes the whole story.

alt: Five sources of unreliability, each linked to its effect on the reader: self-interest makes us doubt the account of conflicts, bias sends us to the other side, limited knowledge makes us infer more, an emotional state suggests distortion, and naivety creates irony.
caption: Naming why a narrator distorts helps you explain what the distortion does.

alt: Six numbered signs: self-contradiction, over-insistence such as "I am perfectly sane", defensive address to an imagined accuser, telling and showing that do not match, contradiction by other characters or documents, and gaps in reasons, motives or events.
caption: Look for a pattern of signs, not a single slip.

after: ## What narrators can and cannot know
alt: Three vantage points. A first-person narrator knows their own mind but not others'. A witness knows the scene but may not know its causes. A narrator telling the story decades later may have forgotten or reshaped events. Some narrators supply what others cannot, and several narrators may contradict one another.
caption: Every narrator sees from somewhere: ask what they could know and what they want to say.

after: ## Worked example 1: a narrator who undermines himself
alt: Four signs of unreliability in the opening of The Tell-Tale Heart. He asks why we will say he is mad; his dashes and repetition sound breathless; he claims he loved the old man though the story is about killing him; and he offers his calm telling as proof of sanity while revealing obsession.
caption: Poe's narrator offers his care as proof of sanity, and the reader sees the reverse.

after: ## Worked example 2: two narrators who contradict
alt: A farmyard sketch shows Lena in the kitchen, able to hear the gate, and Marcus in the barn, able to see the yard. A table sets their accounts side by side: whether Father went out, whether the gate was chained, his mood, and Marcus's attempt to discredit Lena. The reader must weigh both.
caption: Each sibling knows what the other cannot, and neither account is neutral.

after: ## Writing about reliability: a paragraph frame
alt: Five moves for a paragraph: claim how far the narrator can be trusted, quote the evidence, name the source of distortion, state the effect on the reader, and explain the significance. Below, tone is distinguished from reliability: a defensive tone is a clue that needs a second sign.
caption: Claim, evidence, source, effect, significance; and never rest on tone alone.
